Following the cancellation of #JohnGalliano’s retrospective, many were wondering what the new #MetGala theme would be. Today, the new theme was announced: “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday.”

As the title suggests, this year’s theme is about finding beauty in the ordinary and looking at everyday things from a different perspective. Even the most familiar clothes and materials can take on a whole new meaning and artistic value depending on how they are used and reimagined. The exhibition will explore how everyday wardrobe staples, such as jeans and T-shirts, can be transformed into extraordinary works of art through creativity and craftsmanship. It will also look at how materials often considered disposable, such as paper, aluminium and plastic, can become new forms of artistic expression.

When the Met Gala returns on 3 May 2027, how will guests turn the ordinary into something extraordinary?

Long before becoming Iowa’s Governor-Elect, Rob Sand had a career in fashion to finance his way through college, appearing on the runways of some of the industry’s most recognisable names.

His runway credits include: Prada Spring/Summer 2003, Number (N)ine and Giuliano Fujiwara. He also appeared in a Vogue Italia editorial photographed by Steven Meisel. 

From the 2000s Milan runways to the Governor’s Office, Sand makes for an unexpected addition to the fashion archive.

The Fire of Defiance: Alexander McQueen’s Autumn/Winter 1998 “Joan” Collection. A haunting tribute to the sacrifice and immortal spirit of Joan of Arc.

Inspired by the 15th-century French heroine who met her tragic end at the stake in 1431, this legendary London warehouse show explored profound themes of martyrdom and religious persecution. 

Models walked the runway in medieval chainmail armor, sharp tailoring, and garments printed with portraits of the Romanov children, the lost imperial family of Russia’s 1918 tragedy.

For the finale, Erin O’Connor took the stage in a blood-red, beaded dress resembling flayed flesh, standing resilient as a ring of flames erupted around her in a staging inspired by Richard Avedon. 

McQueen was endlessly fascinated by powerful women who faced persecution. 

Wanting to capture the mentality of a woman willing to sacrifice everything for her beliefs, he designed the finale not as a depiction of her demise, but as a triumphant tribute to her immortal defiance.

Martine Rose has officially been named the new Creative Director of Balenciaga, making history as the first woman to lead the 109-year-old French fashion house.

The British designer is no stranger to the maison, having previously worked alongside Demna as a consultant for Balenciaga’s menswear division between 2015 and 2018. Now, she returns with creative control over the entire house, overseeing both menswear and womenswear.

Founded in London in 2007, her label has earned international recognition for its distinctive approach to tailoring, streetwear and British subcultures. 

Following the announcement, fellow British designer Simone Rocha also took to Instagram Stories to congratulate Rose on her new appointment.

Rose will officially begin her new role on November 16, with her debut collection expected in March 2027.

A new chapter for Balenciaga.

Alessandra Ambrosio walked Oscar de la Renta’s Fall/Winter 2000 show in New York at just 18 years old, during the early years of her international modeling career.

Presented in February 2000, the collection took a more relaxed approach to de la Renta’s signature luxury, with cashmere sweaters and colorful knitwear paired with embroidered coats and tailored separates. Eveningwear remained a major focus, with feathered dresses, voluminous ball skirts styled with simple sweaters, and shimmering gowns closing the show.

The Brazilian model was already making her mark on high fashion, walking for houses including Chanel and Fendi that same year. She also appeared in Oscar de la Renta’s Fall/Winter 2000 advertising campaign, years before becoming one of the most recognizable Victoria’s Secret Angels.

Jil Sander’s Fall/Winter 1992 Ready-to-Wear collection, is the definitive blueprint for early ’90s minimalism. 

The “Queen of Less” stripped away 1980s theatrics, shifting focus form, tailoring, and proportions. 

The runway featured Beverly Peele, Christy Turlington, Linda Evangelista, and Claudia Schiffer, who brought effortless energy to the garments. 

By using luxurious, unadorned textiles like fluid wools, rich cashmere, and matte leathers, Sander proved sophistication lies in restraint. 

Decades before “quiet luxury” and “old money aesthetic” trends, this collection laid the groundwork. Its relaxed tailoring, monochromatic palettes, and oversized outerwear remain key inspirations for contemporary designers.

Every season, as the fashion world travels from New York to London, Milan and Paris, @SimbarasheCha is outside the shows, photographing what people are actually wearing on the street for The New York Times. His work also takes him far beyond the Western fashion capitals, from Tokyo to Dakar.

It wasn’t until later in life that Cha realised this was the work he wanted. He spent his twenties trying to make it in music, worked for years in a bank and didn’t buy his first camera until he was 32. 

Getting from there to here took a documentary about the legendary street style photographer Bill Cunningham, years of practice and a few happy accidents. Even now, he says, it hasn’t quite sunk in.

“Every day when I wake up in the morning and I’m brushing my teeth and I am looking at myself in the mirror — this happens every single day without fail — I just remind myself that, oh, this is my job now,” he says. “This is incredibly crazy.”

Cha joins @ImranAmed to talk about why practice makes permanent, the blind spot he had to admit to himself and why the style he looks for is meant to feel within reach.

When Dior published its holiday film on Wednesday, it felt like an antidote to so-called AI slop.

Titled “Christian Dior’s Night in Colour,” the brand touted the film as hand-illustrated, detailing French animator Sylvain Chomet’s process on its website. 

“Technically, we work as they did in the 1940s,” a quote from Chomet read on site. “Everything is cut out, each character is animated separately, and everything is then assembled against the backdrops.”

But online sleuths said they detected discrepancies in the animations. Several noted that while Chomet may indeed have illustrated the primary frames and characters, the team could have used AI to speed up the animation process.

Dior did not immediately respond to BoF’s requests for comment.

@awarodhiang has been named as the British Fashion Council’s Model of the Year.

Awar Odhiang was placed firmly in the fashion conversation after closing Matthieu Blazy’s debut Chanel show in October of 2025 with a contagiously joyful finale. The Canadian model has become a definitive fixture in the industry with covers for Dazed, Harper’s Bazaar France, Vogue France, alongside major campaigns for Chanel, Chloé, Saint Laurent and more. She has used her growing platform to advocate for representation and inclusion of Black models.

“To be recognized as Model of the Year is an incredible honor,” said Odhiang. “I have always believed that you can be both kind and strong, both gentle and resilient. You never have to dim your light to belong, nor lose your softness to prove your strength.”

The panel that selected Odhiang included photographer Campbell Addy, casting director Anita Bitton, and stylist and Wonderland editor in chief Carlos Nazario. They also named Japanese designer @yohjiyamamotoofficial as recipient of the Lifetime Achievement award.

On November 30th, the British Fashion Council will hold their annual Fashion Awards, where Odhiang will receive the honor.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani knows the power of maintaining a signature look in politics. His suits and his trimmed beard, have remained key features of his style — so much so that it was not uncommon to see many men adopting the look as Halloween costumes this year.

So it was something of a shock to see the mayor emerge over the weekend trying something new: a Mamdani mustache.

In a video posted to social media on Monday evening, the mayor revealed his mustache was in honor of @movember, the annual event in support of men's health issues, such as prostate or testicular cancer. In addition to raising both funds and awareness, the Movember campaign, which began in Australia in 2003, also allows men like Mamdani to experiment with a mustache for a month before deciding whether to ditch it when December rolls around. So it remains to be seen whether Mamdani's mo will stick around.

Young Kate Moss rehearsing her runway walk with John Galliano for his SS94 collection, with Galliano personally directing her every movement. 

Presented in October 1993 in an abandoned Parisian mansion, the collection was inspired by Princess Lucretia, a Russian noblewoman who fled her wedding in 1860. With Galliano facing financial difficulties and his career hanging by a thread, the show became a turning point. 

So impressed was Anna Wintour that she personally helped him secure new financial backing, marking one of the most pivotal moments in 90s fashion.

Izumi Suzuki was a Japanese science-fiction writer, actress, model and countercultural icon who became one of the most enigmatic figures of Tokyo’s 1970s underground scene. Born in 1949 in Shizuoka, she moved to Tokyo in 1969, entering the worlds of experimental theatre, underground cinema and avant-garde photography.

She became associated with Shūji Terayama’s experimental theatre company Tenjō Sajiki, alongside artists such as Aquirax Uno and Tadanori Yokoo. She also appeared in Japanese underground cinema, including films by controversial director Kōji Wakamatsu, and was photographed extensively by Nobuyoshi Araki, whose provocative imagery helped establish her distinctive visual legacy.

In 1973, she married free-jazz saxophonist Kaoru Abe, one of Japan’s most radical musicians. Their turbulent relationship ended in divorce in 1977. Abe died from a drug overdose in 1978, leaving Suzuki to raise their daughter.

Following their separation, Suzuki increasingly devoted herself to writing. Her science-fiction stories challenged conventional gender roles, sexuality, marriage and patriarchal society, often portraying women in dystopian, alienated and surreal worlds. Working in a genre largely dominated by men, she developed a distinctly feminist and subversive literary voice. Her collections Terminal Boredom (2021) and Hit Parade of Tears (2023) introduced her work to a much wider international audience through posthumous English translations.

On February 17, 1986, Suzuki died by suicide at just 36. Today, she is remembered not simply as a muse of Japan’s underground, but as a radical literary voice whose explorations of gender, identity and alienation remain remarkably relevant.

Presented in New York in September 1999, Alexander McQueen’s „Eye“ collection for Spring/Summer 2000 marked his first runway show outside London. Inspired partly by London’s Muslim communities, the collection explored the relationship between Western fashion and Middle Eastern cultural references.

The collection combined body-conscious silhouettes, sportswear and fetish-inspired elements with references to Islamic dress, traditional textiles and belly-dancing costumes. 
One of its most distinctive pieces was a metallic interpretation of the traditional yashmak, designed in collaboration with jewellery designer Shaun Leane and constructed from aluminium and Swarovski crystals.

The runway presentation carried strong political undertones. Models walked through a pool of black water, referencing oil and the geopolitical tensions surrounding the Middle East. 
For the finale, performers in burqa-inspired garments were suspended above the runway, creating a theatrical contrast between concealment, exposure and the female body. 
The show also took place during Hurricane Floyd, which was affecting New York that evening. 

„Eye“ remains one of McQueen’s most politically charged collections. Its juxtaposition of Western sexuality and Islamic dress raised questions about gender, cultural identity and the representation of women.

Ultimately, Eye demonstrated McQueen’s ability to use fashion as a medium for political commentary, cultural exploration and theatrical storytelling, extending the runway beyond the presentation of clothing itself.

Jefferson Hack is one of the most influential figures in British fashion publishing. In 1991, aged just 19, he co-founded Dazed & Confused with photographer Rankin, creating a publication that brought fashion, music, art and underground culture together in a way that challenged traditional magazine publishing. He later went on to launch AnOther Magazine in 2001 and Another Man in 2005, helping shape the visual and cultural language of an entire generation. ￼

His personal life became equally connected to the fashion world when he began dating Kate Moss in 2001, after interviewing her for Dazed & Confused. Their relationship brought together two defining figures of early-2000s fashion culture. In 2002, they welcomed their daughter, Lila Grace Moss, who would later follow in her mother’s footsteps and enter the modelling industry. Although their relationship ended, Hack and Moss continued to share a connection through their daughter. ￼

Beyond his relationship with Moss, Hack’s lasting influence lies in the platform he created for emerging photographers, designers, artists and musicians. What began as an independent student publication grew into Dazed Media, becoming an important force in shaping contemporary fashion and youth culture. In 2022, he received the Special Recognition Award for Cultural Curation at the Fashion Awards in recognition of this contribution.

For nearly four decades, the New York-based photographer captured the people, personalities and fleeting moments that defined the city’s streets. Armed with his camera, a bicycle and his signature blue French worker’s jacket, he became an unmistakable presence on the streets of Manhattan.

Working for The New York Times, Cunningham became known for his candid photographs, particularly through his columns On the Street and Evening Hours. Unlike many fashion photographers, he was less interested in celebrities, luxury labels or perfectly staged outfits. His attention belonged to ordinary people, unexpected combinations and individual characters. He photographed fashion as it happened, often without his subjects even noticing.

What made Cunningham truly exceptional was his ability to turn everyday street scenes into a visual record of an entire city. His photographs documented changing generations, cultural movements and the evolution of personal expression. He never considered himself a celebrity and famously valued his independence above money or recognition. When Bill Cunningham took a photograph, he wasn’t simply capturing what people wore – he was capturing the spirit of the moment.

Who should pay to create the next wave of demand for natural diamonds? 💎

The natural diamond industry has a shared interest in stronger consumer demand. But should the responsibility for funding it continue to depend on individual businesses, institutional priorities and periodic fundraising?

In Diamond World, Nicolas Chrétien, Founding Member of the World Diamond Heritage Board (WDHB), proposes a different approach: an independent Diamond Investment Fund that pools contributions across the value chain and invests in initiatives designed to strengthen demand.

His proposed framework raises four important questions for the trade:

🔹 Who contributes? From producing countries and miners to manufacturers, brands, retailers and service providers.

🔹 How much should each contribute? Fair participation, Chrétien argues, need not mean equal contributions.

🔹 Who controls the funds? The proposal separates the institution responsible for raising and governing capital from those executing creative and marketing initiatives.

🔹 How should success be measured? Investment should be assessed by its ability to build consumer desire, strengthen demand and improve retail performance.

One of the article’s most striking illustrations is a potential 1% contribution at each of three stages — rough sales, wholesale and retail — which could theoretically generate more than $1 billion annually.

It’s a proposal, not an established industry mechanism. But it puts a critical question on the table: Can an industry that shares the benefits of demand also share responsibility for creating it?

This holiday season’s big trend appears to be hand-crafted animation. Prada tapped John Pomeroy, famous for his work on Disney and Don Bluth films, to create charming cartoons for their wintry campaign. Loewe is making a collection inspired by Tim Burton’s ‘The Nightmare Before Christmas’ which “resonates deeply with Loewe’s commitment to the handmade.” And Dior released a holiday campaign animated by Sylvain Chomet and voiced by a star-studded cast including Robert Pattinson and Rihanna.

The unsubtle message behind these projects is a rejection of AI, or ‘effort-signalling.’ So, why is Dior’s film receiving backlash?

You can’t pull the wool over animation enthusiasts’ heads; They are extremely devoted to their craft despite the many technological advancements which strive to render them obsolete. Dior and Chomet fans alike quickly noticed alarm-raising abnormalities in the short film; A hand with six fingers, text that was inscrutable when studied closely, suspiciously unnatural movements, and extra folds on one of Monsieur Dior’s eyes. Did Dior release AI slop? 

Dior then released a BTS video with Chomet, perhaps to instill confidence around the processes employed by the animator. But it only made matters worse. Comments on the BTS overwhelmingly focus on its perceived inability to prove that AI was not used. Technical terms like “interpolation” and “in-betweening” began to circulate amongst those who suspected Chomet may have drawn the film’s “key frames” before using AI tools to animate the movements in between them. These criticisms, when viewed next to the widely positive response to Prada and Pomeroy’s recent video, feel particularly damning. 

If the allegations are true, then Dior will have failed in delivering a non-AI product to a fanbase that expects much better. Though the house did not explicitly claim the video was made without AI, the campaign’s conceptual approach comes at a time when other fashion houses are employing analog techniques, especially those related to animation, to convince customers of their holistic approach to high quality craftsmanship. Dior may have just demonstrated to their fans that they’d rather cut corners.

Wool is a staple in fashion, perfect for keeping warm that is both biodegradable and durable 🐑⁠
⁠
But…is it sustainable? Not necessarily 😭 Wool’s a complicated material as so much of modern wool production is tied to animal harm and the devastation of environments.⁠
⁠
The first is obvious: much of the wool industry is tied to animal slaughter practices, which also includes grotesque and painful practices like mulesing and tail docking. While mulesing is now banned in many countries (though not Australia), this remains a welfare concern to be aware of.⁠
⁠
The second is less obvious: grazing animals like sheep can enable environmental degradation. This results in wild animals losing their natural habitat, enabling endangerment and extinction, all as land is cleared to make way for such animals to graze. Intensive sheep farming also results in land degradation and even desertification.⁠
⁠
While standards and certifications do exist, we suggest opting for alternatives from recycled or secondhand wool or plant-based materials like cotton or hemp. Moreover, we strongly encourage cross-referencing @fourpaws.international’s work too, as they offer robust resources on the realities of wool in fashion.⁠

Forget everything you learned on buttoned-up European tastings, the Cape Winelands are about relaxing into the good life in one of the world’s prettiest places. Stretching to the east of Cape Town, they extend into the countryside from the towns of Stellenbosch and Paarl, and include the little village of Franschhoek with its neat rows of vines.

At the foot of Simonsberg, the Babylonstoren estate wraps around a 17th-century Cape Dutch farmstead and comes with exquisite gardens and three restaurants. Make the most of the location and venture into town for a tasting or dinner or explore the fynbos (a unique biome of natural shrubland) of the countryside. There are adventures to be had in the galleries and weekend market at Stellenbosch too, as well as olive oil tastings for those who don’t drink.

It’s always worth combining a Winelands stay with an exploration of wider South Africa. This is a country with so much to experience, after all –  from Big Five safaris in the Kruger National Park to Cape Town’s buzzy neighbourhoods and seaside suburbs.
For something a little different – and utterly unforgettable – head to the lesser-visited Cederberg Wilderness Area. Around three hours north of the Winelands, it’s a place to hike below vast skies towards 10,000 year-old rock art and taste the local rooibos tea.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art will devote its next blockbuster fashion exhibition to showcasing the ordinary. Or as the title has it, the “extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday.” Think bluejeans, puffer jackets and white T-shirts — even paper, plastic and Bubble Wrap — reimagined through the lens of high fashion.

The announcement comes two months after the museum’s Costume Institute bowed to public pressure and postponed its planned spring exhibition, an examination of the work of the designer John Galliano. The show set off a firestorm of criticism after it was revealed in The New York Times, because of the designer’s history of antisemitic remarks.

On the surface, the new exhibition, for which the Met Gala serves as a ceremonial opening night, seems deliberately uncontentious and a clear contrast with the Galliano show. It’s refreshing to see a brand commission a real artist to create something that takes time, patience and genuine skill. Rather than just revisiting the archives, Piccioli approached Cristobal Balenciaga’s #HauteCouture legacy through craftsmanship, construction and volume.

Perhaps we never got to see the full extent of what @pppiccioli could have achieved at @balenciaga . But for a brief moment he reminded us what made it so extraordinary in the first place.

India’s restaurant business has long favoured the extensive menu, with something for everyone at the table. A growing number of newer establishments are challenging that formula, building businesses around a single dish or a tightly defined food category.

The economics are part of the appeal. A smaller offering can simplify procurement, reduce kitchen complexity, and help restaurants control wastage. Specialisation can also support premium pricing and give a brand a distinct identity in a crowded market.

But the model has its limits. A narrow menu leaves less room to accommodate different preferences, and a popular opening can be difficult to convert into a sustainable business.

Deepawali marks the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile, following the abduction of his wife and a long battle with Ravana. It all ends with the happy homecoming of the divine couple, Ram and Sita, along with Lakshmana. For centuries, people have celebrated this day as Deepawali , a welcome to the divine into our homes.

But the story of Ram travelled far beyond India. Through ancient trade routes, religious travellers and storytellers, it reached Southeast Asia, where each culture gave it its own identity.

In Thailand, it became the Ramakien; in Cambodia, the Reamker; in Laos, the Phra Lak Phra Lam; and in Indonesia, the Kakawin Ramayana. In Myanmar, the story also developed its own tradition, with the earliest known written Burmese version, Rama Thagyin, dating to 1775.

Interestingly, every adaptation has its own cultural elements and stories. Even within India, the Ramayana has hundreds of tellings across languages and communities. As A. K. Ramanujan explores in Three Hundred Ramayanas, one story can take many forms. Ramleela remains a major festive tradition, bringing the epic to life through local theatre, music and performance.

Ramnagar Ramleela, in particular, is a tradition in which an entire town becomes a stage, creating a deep connection between the story and the people of the land.

And so, every festive season, the narrative returns as a remembrance of Ram’s homecoming, a story of the divine couple, their journey and the enduring message of good over evil and right over wrong.

Deepawali is closely associated with the worship of Śrī Lakṣmī in many parts of India and is widely known as the festival of lights.

According to popular belief, Lakṣmī descends from the heavens on this night, moving from home to home and blessing those where she finds devotion, respect and positivity. Deepavali falls on Amavasya, the darkest night of the lunar month, when homes are lit with lamps, bringing light into the darkness.

But the history behind the goddess we worship today goes much further back.

The image of Śrī Lakṣmī as we know her today developed over centuries, through different texts, beliefs and traditions. Śrī and Lakṣmī have overlapping yet distinguishable histories in early texts, with their identities becoming increasingly intertwined over time.

The word Śrī itself has a long history. In early Vedic literature, it carries associations of splendour, beauty, prosperity and flourishing. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Śrī emerges as a divine figure, embodying many of these associations.

Her journey through Vedic literature offers a fascinating insight into the many layers of meaning behind the goddess we recognise today as Śrī Lakṣmī.

Every piece has a story.

In 1893, Chicago hosted the World’s Columbian Exposition, a huge international fair commemorating the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s arrival in the Americas. Millions came to see inventions, grand buildings and exhibits promising a glimpse of the wider world. Among the most popular was Cairo Street, a reconstructed Egyptian neighbourhood with shops, camel rides, performances and a mosque. 

Five times a day, the adhan sounded from its minaret. The organizers were pleasantly surprised to see Muslims answer the call and gather to pray. Their worship became an attraction in its own right, with tourists watching from an interior gallery. 

The mosque was modelled on Sultan Qaytbay’s funerary mosque in Cairo’s Northern Cemetery, but its minaret replicated that of Abu Bakr ibn Muzhir’s mosque in Cairo’s Old City. Egypt’s ruler at the time, Khedive Abbas II, expressed concerned for the mosque because he had previously seen a mosque replica desecrated at the 1889 Paris exposition but the promoter assured him that the Chicago mosque would remain sacred and serve the Egyptian Muslim community there. 

Other mosques stood in the Ottoman and Javanese villages but heavily integrated into the amusement landscape. The Javanese mosque served the people brought from present-day Indonesia. Instead of a call from a minaret, a large drum called a bedug summoned worshippers. The Turkish mosque stood within the Ottoman village and opened for Friday prayers before the fair officially began. A contemporary account says tourists could enter only after prayers had finished. 

Muslims from Algeria, Egypt, Nubia, Persia, Sudan, Tunisia, Turkey and India came to visit and work at the fair. Some stayed and settled in Chicago. When the exhibition ended, the temporary mosques were dismantled, but the city’s Muslim communities continued to grow.

What does political power mean when you cannot protect the people you love?

At just 37, Humza Yousaf became Scotland’s youngest First Minister, the first person of colour to hold the office and the first Muslim to lead a Western democracy. But in October 2023, while holding Scotland’s highest political office, he found himself desperately trying to bring his wife’s parents home from Gaza, where they were trapped under Israeli bombardment.

In today’s @BrownHistoryPodcast episode, we sit down with Humza Yousaf to discuss his book, ‘Under Fire: My Family’s Escape from Gaza and The Cost of Leadership,’ and those four weeks of fear and uncertainty. We also talk about his Pakistani heritage, belonging in Scotland, and what his experience reveals about representation and the limits of political power. Link in Bio.

Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass to become the next mayor of Los Angeles.

Born in Kerala, India, Raman moved to the United States at six and grew up in Massachusetts. She studied at Harvard and MIT, trained as an urban planner and worked with low-income communities in India before becoming involved in housing and homelessness advocacy in Los Angeles.

In 2020, she became the first South Asian elected to the Los Angeles City Council. Six years later, she has won the race to lead the second-largest city in the United States, marking a historic moment.

Raman has stated that she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza and described the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement as a "legitimate form of peaceful protest."
